title: Seedfall
subtitle: Comparing Means Assignment · t-test, ANOVA, pairwise/Tukey
story: The wood is going gold and cold, and the first snow is a day off, maybe less. You are a jay, and before the white comes you have one task that matters more than all your others: work out which trees here grow the best nuts, and cache their seeds in the best ground — because the few you never dig up again will be the forest your grandchildren fly through. You begin in the crown of the Mother Oak, where a strange grid of empty niches glows in the trunk — you don't yet know what it wants. So you set off the way a jay reads a forest: tree to tree, up and down and across, weighing the wood as you go.

done.title: The wood has told you true
done.body: You know it now — the reliable ground, and the two kinds of tree whose nuts are honestly the best. The survey holds together, careful all the way down.

escapeDone.title: The long cache
escapeDone.body: The tiers hold; the cache-frame seals warm in the Mother Oak's heartwood. You tuck the last seed away as the snow begins, and fold your wings into the roost — the wood around you already, quietly, the shape of the forest to come.

coverPrompt: Minimalist stylised thumbnail poster of a single jay perched before one great ancient oak in an autumn wood, a scatter of acorns below and one warm amber glow low in the tree's hollow. Designed to read clearly as a small thumbnail: one bold, simple, high-contrast silhouette, iconic and uncluttered, minimal fine detail. Flat, limited palette: deep teal, russet, and one warm amber glow. Soft film grain, painterly but clean with simple geometric shapes. Strong negative space, single centred focal subject. No people, no text, no lettering, no logos. Square composition.

debrief.title: How the wood worked
debrief.intro: The whole wood was open to you from the first, but the survey had its order: each reading waited on the one before it, the way a careful comparison waits on a fair test. You weighed groves and kinds by choosing the honest test each time — a t-test where the nuts behaved, a rank test where a few gusher trees would have fooled the average, ANOVA and its follow-up to name which kind, and a corrected read that refused to crown a winner over a tie. And you sealed the cache not with numbers but with your wings, grouping the kinds by the heights you'd flown among. Here is how each part embodied the comparison of means.

question.prompt: You start by weighing nuts in two neighbouring stands — the sunlit Sunhollow and the shaded, brook-side Downbriar. Are Sunhollow's nuts genuinely heavier, or does the sunny stand just look fuller?
options: No — the two groves' nuts aren't significantly different
Yes — a significant difference; Sunhollow grows the heavier nuts
Yes — but Downbriar grows the heavier nuts
You can't test it — the data are non-normal, so no test applies
It's significant only if you skip the normality check first
They differ in oil content, but not in nut weight
The variances are unequal, so the difference is untestable

feedback.correct: Certified — Sunhollow's nuts run heavier than Downbriar's (about 31.1 g vs 28.3 g), a real difference.
wrong: Keep only grove %in% c('Sunhollow','Downbriar') and parameter == 'kernel_mass_g', then compare the two groves.
Check the assumptions first: a Shapiro test (within each grove) and a Levene test (across the two) decide whether a t-test is fair here. Both pass — so the t-test is the honest, most powerful tool.
The two groves do differ — look again at which grove's mean nut weight is the higher one.

question.prompt: Winter nuts must be rich and oily. You test a dry ridge (Larkspur) against the boggy fen (Emberfen), where a few trees are gushers. Which grove is the reliably oilier ground — and which test is honest for data shaped like this?
options: A t-test — significant; Emberfen is the oilier grove
The two groves aren't significantly different
A Wilcox test — significant; Larkspur is the reliably oilier grove
A Wilcox test — significant; but Emberfen is oilier
A t-test — significant; Larkspur is oilier
The data are normal, so a plain t-test is fine
A Kruskal test — the right tool for these two groves

feedback.correct: Certified — Emberfen's few gusher trees pull its average up, but most of its nuts are poor. The oil is skewed, so the rank-based Wilcox test is the honest call: the typical Larkspur tree (median ~14.2%) beats the typical Emberfen tree (~10.5%).
wrong: Filter to grove %in% c('Larkspur','Emberfen') and parameter == 'oil_content_pct', then check the shape of Emberfen's readings before you pick a test.

The Shapiro test fails on Emberfen — a few gusher trees make it wildly right-skewed — so the mean (and a t-test) is dragged upward and names the wrong grove. Which two-group test uses ranks, not the mean?
Compare the medians, not the means: the outliers inflate Emberfen's average, but the ordinary Larkspur tree is oilier. A Kruskal test is for >2 groups; you have two.

question.prompt: The last question, and the hardest: which kinds truly make the BEST nuts for the cache? Compare all four, pair by pair — but account for having compared so many. What does the honest reading say?
options: All four kinds differ — rank them and cache the single best
Only green oak is best; the other three are tied below it
green oak, golden aspen and red maple are tied at the top
green oak and golden aspen are tied at the top; red maple and silver birch are the lower tier
red maple and silver birch are the best pair
None of the kinds differ — cache any of them
golden aspen alone is best

feedback.correct: Certified — corrected for all six comparisons, the kinds fall into two honest tiers: green oak and golden aspen tied at the top (you can't separate them), red maple and silver birch below. Cache both top kinds.
wrong: Filter to parameter == 'nut_quality_index' and compare the four kinds pairwise — anova_test then tukey_hsd(value ~ leaf_colour), which corrects for the multiple comparisons.
You're running six comparisons at once. Uncorrected, small gaps look 'significant' by chance — apply the correction (Tukey / a p.adjust), and watch which apparent differences vanish.
Two apparent gaps are just noise: green vs gold at the top, and red vs silver at the bottom, both collapse once corrected. Don't crown a single winner over a genuine tie.
